content.text: CLAUDE.md loads into every Claude Code session, so every line costs a little attention on every task. A long file that explains the architecture and lists every rule doesn't make Claude follow the project better: Claude can read the code itself, and the lines that matter get lost. Keep the file for what Claude can't see in the repo, and move the rest to rules, skills or hooks.

A team's CLAUDE.md started as twenty lines. Every time Claude missed something, someone added a paragraph: an architecture overview, the folder tree, every lint rule, a forty-step release procedure. Now it's 600 lines, and the one convention that keeps breaking, "throw

, never raw strings", sits in the middle next to a folder tree that's two refactors out of date. Someone rewrites it as "IMPORTANT: NEVER THROW RAW STRINGS". Claude starts wrapping errors in test helpers too, where the team wanted plain assertions.
"The more Claude knows about the project, the better it follows it, so CLAUDE.md should document the architecture and every rule." Smart teams believe this for good reasons:

items.text: Onboarding docs work that way for people: a new hire with a thorough guide makes fewer mistakes.
generates a CLAUDE.md from the codebase, which looks like an invitation to describe it, though the docs add that from there "the work is mostly removing lines".
Older models sometimes did need things spelled out, and loud emphasis once helped.
When Claude misses a rule, adding text is the fastest fix at hand.

content.text: The half-truth: CLAUDE.md really is the place for what Claude must know in every session. But "every session" is exactly the problem. What's useful on one task is noise on the next, and Claude can already find most of it.
Every line is in every session

files in your working directory and above it load at launch, and Claude Code re-sends the full context, including them, with every request. Anthropic's best-practices guide says each line "takes a little of Claude's attention on every task, whether it's relevant or not". The memory guide gives the size target: under 200 lines per file, because "Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence." And if two instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily, a risk that grows when nobody prunes the file.
CLAUDE.md is also context, not configuration. It arrives as a user message after the system prompt, and Claude "tries to follow it, but there's no guarantee of strict compliance".

Claude starts each task by reading code, and the docs say current models find your file layout, conventions, test framework and how existing components are built, "usually faster than you could explain them". That's why "Describe your architecture and file layout in CLAUDE.md" is on the docs' list of advice you can stop following. The
checkup proposes trims along the same lines: directory layouts, dependency lists and architecture overviews go; pitfalls, rationale and conventions that differ from tool defaults stay.
Before writing a line, the docs suggest asking: could Claude find this by reading the code, and would it actually go and look? If both answers are yes, leave it out. What passes the test is short:

items.text: How to confirm work: the exact test, typecheck and lint commands, and how to run one test file
Places where the code misleads: an old pattern that new code must not copy, a directory that looks unused but isn't
Decisions that aren't in the repo, such as which error helper the team settled on
Anything you've had to correct twice

content.text: The docs list IMPORTANT and ALL CAPS among habits from older models. Current models follow a plainly worded line, and piling on emphasis "mostly makes Claude over-apply the rule". If Claude keeps ignoring a line, either the file is long enough that the line gets lost, or it's a rule with no exceptions, which belongs in a hook.
The same file, before and after

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
# Architecture
Next.js app. Pages in src/app/, components in src/components/,
API routes in src/app/api/, helpers in src/lib/.
Stack: React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Prisma, Vitest.

# Folder structure
src/app/ src/components/ src/lib/ prisma/ tests/ ...

# Rules
- IMPORTANT: ALWAYS write clean, readable code
- Use TypeScript for all new files
- NEVER THROW RAW STRINGS!!! Use the error helpers.

# Release process
1. Pull main. 2. Bump the version. 3. ... (38 more steps)

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
# Commands
- Install: pnpm install
- One test file: pnpm vitest run path/to/file.test.ts
- Typecheck: pnpm tsc --noEmit

# Conventions
- Throw AppError from src/lib/errors.ts, never raw strings
- src/legacy/ is still live; don't copy its patterns

# Gotchas
- Integration tests need DATABASE_URL (see .env.example)
- After editing prisma/schema.prisma, run pnpm db:generate

content.text: Everything in the first version's top half is visible in the repo. "Write clean code" can't be checked, and the release steps matter only when you release. The second version holds commands Claude needs to check its own work, one convention it couldn't guess and two traps it would hit.
A rule that matters for one part of the codebase goes in
filter. It loads only when Claude reads, writes or edits a matching file:

blocks.code:
---
paths:
  - "src/app/api/**/*.ts"
---
- Validate request bodies with the zod schemas in src/lib/schemas/
- Every new endpoint needs an entry in openapi.yaml

How to apply it in your project
Let the checkup propose cuts for content Claude can derive from the codebase. Review each one; you decide what goes.

items.title: Apply the two-question test to every line

content.text: Could Claude find it in the code, and would it look? If yes to both, delete it. Keep commands, traps and decisions.

items.title: Move area rules and procedures out

content.text: Put rules for one directory in
, and long procedures in a skill.
If a line has emphasis because Claude must never break it, enforce it with a hook or a deny rule and drop the caps.
Review CLAUDE.md changes in pull requests, and run
now and then to catch stale or contradicting lines. Start a fresh session to load the new version.

items.text: CLAUDE.md loads into every session, so every line costs attention on every task, relevant or not.
Aim for under 200 lines; longer files consume more context and reduce adherence.
Don't describe the architecture or folder layout; Claude reads the repo.
Keep commands, misleading spots, decisions that aren't in the repo and repeated corrections.
, procedures to skills and must-never rules to hooks.
